stops.name: Issus, the Great King in flight and the captured queen mother
stops.campa: Darius, cutting behind Alexander onto this narrow coastal plain, is broken when Alexander drives his companions straight at the Persian center; Darius abandons shield, bow, and royal cloak to escape on a fresher horse, leaving his mother, wife, and children behind in the captured camp. Alexander and Hephaestion go to promise the women safety; the old queen Sisygambis, mistaking the taller Hephaestion for the king, bows to him first and is covered in shame at her error. Alexander raises her, saying she has not erred, for Hephaestion too is an Alexander, and claims Darius's own tent that night, remarking that this, it seems, is what it is to be a king.
stops.quote: You did not err, mother; for he too is Alexander.
stops.quote_source: Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 3.12.17 ('non errasti, mater; nam et hic Alexander est'); Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.37

stops.name: Tyre, the dream of the god and the causeway
stops.campa: Tyre, an island fortress with walls rising straight from the sea, refuses Alexander entry even to sacrifice to its god Melqart, whom the Greeks call Heracles and count among Alexander's own ancestors. He answers with a mole of stone, timber, and rubble driven straight across the strait toward the walls, under constant fire from the towers and fire-ships of the Tyrians. In the city, the high priest dreams that Melqart is leaving Tyre to walk beside Alexander's camp; in Alexander's own camp, the seer Aristander reads a satyr dancing on his shield as a Greek pun: sa Tyros, Tyre is yours.

stops.name: Tyre, the king descends in a vessel of glass
stops.campa: To see with his own eyes what the Tyrians have built beneath the waves against his causeway, Alexander has a great barrel of clear glass made, sealed and chained, and has himself lowered into the harbor depths. Around him move the shapes of the deep, vast and voracious, feeding without pity on the small and the weak, and the king watches in silence a long while before signaling to be drawn up. When he stands again on his own deck he tells his officers plainly what he has learned of the world below the world, and it unsettles them more than any siege.
stops.quote: The world is damned and lost: the great and powerful fish devour the small fry.
stops.quote_source: The Alexander Romance, glass-vessel descent (Pseudo-Callisthenes and its vernacular daughters); the moral of the great fish devouring the small is the medieval Western retelling's, not the Greek recension's

stops.name: Gaza, the wound and the dust of Achilles
stops.campa: Batis, eunuch commander of Gaza, holds the last fortress before Egypt and answers Alexander's summons with silent defiance, trusting his high mound and his tunnels dug under the siege-works. Three assaults fail; in the second, a bolt from a catapult drives through Alexander's shield and breastplate into his shoulder, and he fights on wounded. When the walls fall at last after two months, Batis is taken alive, and Alexander, remembering Achilles dragging Hector behind his chariot beneath the walls of Troy, has a cord run through Batis's heels and drags him living around the city until he dies.

stops.name: Memphis, the crowning of the pharaoh
stops.campa: Egypt, chafing two centuries under Persian tax and Persian gods, opens its gates without a blow; the satrap Mazaces surrenders Pelusium and Memphis both, and the crowds hail Alexander as liberator. In Memphis he sacrifices to Apis, the sacred bull the Persians had mocked and, some say, killed, and the priests of Ptah anoint him upon the ancient throne with the double crown, naming him Son of Ra and Beloved of Amun in the unbroken formula they have given every pharaoh for three thousand years. He holds games there, Greek athletes and poets performing before the oldest kingship on earth.

stops.name: Alexandria, the city outlined in barley and devoured by birds
stops.campa: Between the sea and Lake Mareotis, Alexander walks the ground himself and marks out the streets, the agora, the sanctuaries of a city to bear his name, in the shape of a soldier's cloak. Having no chalk, the engineers pour out the army's barley meal along his lines; before the walls can even be surveyed, birds descend on the outline from the river and the marsh in uncounted thousands and eat every grain. The seers, watching Alexander's face darken, tell him the sign is good beyond reading: the city will feed multitudes from every nation and never want for bread.

stops.name: Siwa, the oracle names the son of god
stops.campa: Across days of waterless desert and blinding wind, twice saved, the tradition says, by ravens or serpents sent to guide the lost column and by a sudden storm of rain, Alexander reaches the green spring-fed oasis and the oracle-shrine of Ammon, whom the Greeks read as Zeus. The priest, they say confused by his own Greek, greets him not as Ammon's servant but as his son. Inside the sanctuary alone, Alexander asks his questions and hears his answers; he tells his companions afterward only that he has heard what was agreeable to his wishes, and never repeats the rest to any man alive.
stops.quote: I have heard what was agreeable to my wishes.
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.4 (reported as Alexander's own account of the oracle); cf. Plutarch, Life of Alexander 27

stops.name: Gaugamela, the eclipse and the broken center
stops.campa: Eleven nights before the battle the moon rises full and turns to blood over the Persian camp and goes dark; the Magi read it as ruin for the king of kings, and Alexander tells his own frightened men it foretells a Persian, not a Macedonian, eclipse. When Parmenion urges a night attack against Darius's far larger host, Alexander refuses outright: he will not steal a victory. At dawn he drives a wedge through the weakened Persian center exactly where he chose to strike; Darius flees the field a second time, and the empire of Cyrus and Darius the Great effectively ends before noon.
stops.quote: I will not steal my victory.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 31 (Perrin), to Parmenio on the eve of the battle; Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.10 reports the same refusal indirectly

stops.name: Babylon, the gates opened to the conqueror
stops.campa: Babylon, greatest city the army has seen, sends out its priests and nobles with garlands, gifts, and open gates rather than face a siege; the Persian satrap Mazaeus himself surrenders the citadel. Alexander enters in state along the processional way to Esagila, sacrifices to Bel-Marduk as the Chaldean priests direct, and orders the temple, left to ruin under Xerxes, rebuilt at his own expense. He confirms Mazaeus in his satrapy, the first Persian so honored, and lets his weary men rest a month in a city whose luxury, the Macedonian officers mutter, may prove more dangerous than any Persian army.

stops.name: Susa, the treasure of the Achaemenids
stops.campa: Susa yields without a blow and with it the accumulated treasury of the House of Cyrus and Darius: fifty thousand talents of gold and silver bullion, dyed Hermione purple worth its own weight untouched for a hundred and eighty years, and the royal chair itself, on which Alexander sits, his feet too short for the Persian footstool the servants have brought, so that a page slides a table under them instead. Among the spoil Alexander finds the bronze statues of the tyrannicides Harmodius and Aristogeiton, carried off by Xerxes from Athens a century and a half before, and sends them home.

stops.name: Persepolis, the palace burned
stops.campa: Ceremonial capital of the kings, Persepolis surrenders its treasury of one hundred and twenty thousand talents and is given over to four months of plunder, the harshest sack of the whole campaign, Alexander tells his men, in payment for Xerxes's burning of Athens a century and a half before. At a night's banquet the Athenian courtesan Thais rises, torch in hand, and calls on the company to finish what Xerxes began and burn the palace of Xerxes down; Alexander, they say, is the first to fling his own torch onto the cedar roof-beams, and the fire spreads from hall to hall until dawn.

stops.name: The road to Hecatompylos, the death of the Great King
stops.campa: Fleeing east from his own collapsing empire, Darius is seized by his kinsman Bessus and the satrap Nabarzanes, bound in golden fetters, and carried in a covered ox-cart as Alexander's cavalry closes the distance in a killing forced march. Overtaken at last, the conspirators stab Darius and abandon him and flee; a Macedonian soldier finds the last king of Persia dying alone in the wagon. Alexander comes too late to speak with him, but covers the body with his own cloak and sends it on to Persepolis for burial among the tombs of his royal predecessors, a king honoring a king.
